19880-voice-production-in-singing-and-sp:
Voice Production in Singing and Speaking rests, its title says, on scientific principles. Wesley Mills, a physiologist, wrote it. Its illustrations contrast healthy and diseased throats for singers. One plate shows a larynx pale with tuberculosis. A weakened muscle leaves the vocal band slack on one side. The voice turns uncertain and harsh as a result. Such images impress the normal by contrast, Mills explains.

Voice teachers of the era craved anatomy to replace guesswork. Laryngoscope pictures brought the singing throat into view. Mills treats breath, cords, and resonance as one machine. Singers and speakers both get exercises from the science. The book marks elocution's turn toward the laboratory. Its plates remain striking medical documents.
20571-woman-s-work-in-music:
Arthur Elson's Woman's Work in Music, published in 1903, surveys what women had done in music and compares it with the work of men. Elson was a music critic, and he writes with a critic's store of examples. The question of women composers was much argued in his day.

He notes a curious fact about the Church of Rome. The church admits no women to a share in its services, yet it has made a woman, Saint Cecilia, the patron saint of music. The religions of the ancient world paid women even more homage in this art. Elson builds his case from such history.
21072-the-pirate-island-a-story-of-the-s:
A gale on the Essex coast opens Harry Collingwood's South Pacific tale. Rescuers pull an orphan boy from a sinking ship, and a fisherman adopts him. Years later, young people sail for Australia aboard the Galatea. Fire breaks out on the return voyage, and all aboard take to the boats.

Their rescuers turn out to be pirates, who carry them to an island base full of captured ships. Learning that one prisoner has built his own fast yacht, the pirate captain orders a new fast ship built. The captives also find a reef of gold, then flee in the new ship as an earthquake and eruption kill their pursuers.
21084-jokes-for-all-occasions-selected-a:
Jokes for All Occasions was published in New York by Edward J. Clode in 1921 and 1922. An unnamed speaker, billed as one of America's foremost public speakers, selected it. After-dinner speakers were its market. The jokes are sorted by topic so a speaker can find one fast.

The opening section covers absentmindedness. It starts with a man who grabs a woman's umbrella on a street car. He meets her again that day, carrying eight repaired umbrellas of his own. Other tales mock inventors, clergymen, and forgetful husbands. The humour is gentle, dated, and built for retelling aloud at banquets and club nights.
21456-the-cruise-of-the-dainty-or-roving:
Two brothers endure a flat calm at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Cruise of the Dainty. Their ship roves the Pacific, where many islanders had good cause to hate Europeans. Traders had lured folk aboard, shut them below, and sold them as slaves in Peru.

On deck, mates set hands to mats, rope yarns, knots, and splices in the heat. The Dainty meets wary islands, bad weather, and worse crews on other ships. Kingston keeps the book short, but he packs it with the ways of Pacific voyaging. Honest dealing, he shows, is rare and precious in those seas.
21457-the-cruise-of-the-mary-rose-or-her:
Kingston's The Cruise of the Mary Rose wears the dress of a boys' sea story, but its heart lies elsewhere. Much of the book treats the work of Christian missions in the Pacific. A thin plot links long extracts from reports by mission staff and naval officers.

Those reports tell of island life, new churches, and the hardships of the work. Kingston, a devout man, writes here with extra zeal for the cause. He does not hide the ugly customs the missions fought against. Readers who care for mission history will find rich, first-hand matter, gathered from men who saw it.
21542-spirit-and-music:
H. Ernest Hunt argues that music is a spiritual art in Spirit and Music, published in 1922. Hunt lectured on psychology at London schools for music teachers. His other books treat nerve control, self training, and the influence of thought.

He notes that, strictly, no sound exists until the brain renders the ear's message. Chapters treat the spirit of music, its place in life, and the conditions of inspiration. The interpreter, the teacher, and the soul of song each get a chapter. Hunt closes on pure music and the purpose of art, in a thoughtful Edwardian key.
21552-masterman-ready-or-the-wreck-of-th:
Captain Marryat wrote Masterman Ready, or the Wreck of the Pacific, in 1841 for young readers. A captain watches the helm with care as his ship runs before a heavy gale. He sings a low sea song while he studies the sky.

Ready, the old seaman of the title, guides a wrecked family on a Pacific island. The book was Marryat's nineteenth, and its plainer style suits its child audience. Storm, wreck, and the slow building of a home fill the tale. Generations of children learned seamanship and grit from Ready's steady, knowing hands.
21714-the-red-eric:
Captain Dunning, owner of a South Sea whale ship, bursts with color from the first page of this Ballantyne novel. His whiskers are red, his coat is blue, and his waistcoat is yellow. He is abrupt in speech but kind at heart, and his eyes twinkle more often than they flash. The Red Eric is his ship, and her crew fills out the tale.

Whaling in the South Seas means long months of work, danger, and strange sights far from home. Ballantyne keeps the captain's good humor at the center of the story. Around him he builds a crew's life at sea: storms, whales, ports, and the bonds that hold sailors together.
22252-rollo-on-the-atlantic:
Jacob Abbott sent his most famous boy travelling in Rollo on the Atlantic. Rollo, about twelve years old, makes the voyage to Europe under extraordinary circumstances. He goes alone, or rather with no one appointed to take care of him. A kind uncle and fellow passengers must fill the gap on the long crossing.

Abbott fills the steamship days with lessons on ships, the sea, ports, and manners. Rollo asks the questions young readers would ask, and grown-ups answer them patiently. The Rollo books taught geography and conduct to millions of American children. This volume opens the European tour that carried Rollo through England, France, Switzerland, and Holland.
22815-the-philippine-islands-a-political:
Spanish rule comes under sharp attack in The Philippine Islands, a wide survey of the islands' politics, land, peoples, and trade. The writer charges Spain with chasing new dominion like a mania while neglecting roads, schools, and commerce at home in the colony. Money spent on fruitless expeditions, he argues, could have built wealth many times over.

Around that argument sits a full portrait of the archipelago. Geography, native customs, government, and resources each get their turn, giving readers of the era a single volume for a distant place. The book matters now as evidence of how the islands were described to English-speaking readers, praise, blame, and bias included. It should be read with that slant in mind.
23162-no-great-magic:
Fritz Leiber checks the callboard in No Great Magic. The dresser puts the question quietly to Siddy. Which play tonight, Anderson's Elizabeth or Shakespeare's Macbeth? The callboard says Macbeth, yet Miss Nefer is preparing Elizabeth. She has just sent him to fetch the red wig.

A dresser who has served every great stage magician of history narrates Leiber's tale, and theatre itself becomes the spell. Costumes, wigs, and two plays competing for one night carry an argument about where magic really lives. Leiber loved actors, swords, and cats in roughly that order, and his backstage knowledge glows here. The story is a connoisseur's piece, greasepaint over genuine wonder, by a writer who never separated the two.
23260-the-two-whalers-or-adventures-in-t:
The Two Whalers, or Adventures in the Pacific is a sea adventure tale. Its warmest moment is a reunion. A sailor gives his name as Bill, then grips the narrator's hand and wrings it till it nearly comes off, half laughing and half crying with pleasure.

He is sure he has found his brother Jack. At once the questions pour out: how are father and mother, Susan and Jane, Mary and Dick, and little Tommy? The scene sets family feeling at the heart of whaling adventure. Readers get the Pacific whaling world of ships, ports, and chance meetings between men long lost to home.
a-trip-to-scarborough-and-the-critic: Sheridan pairs his comedy A Trip to Scarborough with his immortal farce The Critic — the tale of Mr. Puff and his disastrous play. Two delights from the wittiest playwright of the age. Laughter, guaranteed. Town fops, Irish bluster, and Mr. Puff's theatrical disasters provide an evening of pure fun.

This progress report describes the team's pragmatic approach to AI-driven operational excellence — building AI that actually works for running the network. Real-world lessons from teaching machines to mind the pipes.
doe-osti-3602550-holographic-aerosol-mon: Airborne microbes drift invisibly through the air we breathe. The HAMBAEX interim report covers a field campaign using a holographic aerosol monitor to spot biological aerosols. The instrument films tiny airborne particles in 3-D, catching living ones other sensors miss.
five-weeks-in-a-balloon-or-journeys-and-: Jules Verne's 1863 Five Weeks in a Balloon: the first extraordinary voyage. Africa crossed by air. The adventure novel's birth. A timeless classic, verne's first extraordinary voyage, africa by balloon, a timeless classic, Verne, 1863, balloon, Africa.
giles-an-address-on-the-need-for-medical: An address on the need for medical teaching on birth control, microform, by Giles. The doctor's plea. This book preserves that address. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClassificationU:
File 105-82555 was the FBI's headquarters file on Lee Harvey Oswald, and this memorandum of October 22, 1964, belongs to it. By then the Warren Report had been public for a month, and the Bureau's Oswald paperwork was still growing.

The archive's filing heading for the memo concerns classification, the Bureau's judgments about what in the Oswald record stayed secret and why. Classification fights decided what researchers could see for thirty years, until the Review Board of the 1990s overruled many of them. The single memo is preserved as a page of the main file, from the first year of its long secrecy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
Dusko Doder reported for the Washington Post on a scandal closing in on Canadian Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau. Canada's security forces stood accused of bugging, break-ins, and dirty tricks against people at home. Doder framed the affair as Canada's own version of Watergate.

The comparison tells readers how serious the charges were. A democratic government was facing proof that its security services had broken the law in the name of security. The article preserves an American view of that crisis as it broke, when the scale of the abuses was still coming to light.
govdocs-archive_org-the-hypostasis-of-th:
The Hypostasis of the Archons is a Gnostic treatise found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt. Roger Aubrey Bullard's edition gives the Coptic text with translation and commentary, prepared with Martin Krause.

The treatise retells Genesis from the Gnostic side. The archons, proud rulers of the material world, make man, envy his spirit, and send the flood, while a higher God works to save him. Bullard's commentary explains the language and the ideas line by line. For students of early Christianity and Gnosticism, the edition is a cornerstone: text, translation, and guidance in one volume.
history-of-cuba-or-notes-of-a-traveller-: History of Cuba, or Notes of a Traveller in the Tropics, political and otherwise. The island's history. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
laughter-an-essay-on-the-meaning-of-the-:
Henri Bergson wrote Laughter as an essay on the meaning of the comic. Bergson taught at the Collège de France and belonged to the French Institute. Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell made this authorized English translation.

Bergson himself revised the translation in detail, the preface stresses. He asks why people laugh and what laughter does in society. Comic figures, he argues, often act like stiff machines. That stiffness, seen in a living person, provokes laughter. His short book became a classic text for anyone studying comedy. Later writers on humor still argue with Bergson's machine idea. His examples from stage comedy keep the theory concrete.
laxd-la-saga-translated-from-the-iceland:
Muriel A. C. Press translated Laxdæla Saga from the Icelandic for J. M. Dent in 1899. The saga opens with Ketill Flatnose and his descendants in the ninth century. His sons prepare to leave Norway for Iceland.

Ketill himself sails to Scotland around the year 890. Unn follows to Iceland and divides her land among kin. Weddings, births, and feuds fill the chapters that follow. The saga traces one great family's fortunes across generations. English readers meet Iceland's classic prose tradition in a clear Victorian translation. Feuds over love and honor drive the saga's best-known episodes. Press's version keeps names, dates, and places carefully ordered.
love-and-freindship-sic:
Love and Freindship gathers Jane Austen's early writings, spelled just as she spelled them. Austen wrote these pieces in her teens, long before her famous novels. The title work is a tale in letters, from Laura to Marianne and others. A second unfinished novel in letters, Lesley Castle, follows it here.

Young Austen mocks the weepy novels of her day with wild delight. Her heroines faint, elope, steal, and die of grief in quick order. Every letter piles absurd trouble on absurd trouble. Yet the wit is sharp, and the comic timing already feels masterly. These pages show the future author of Pride and Prejudice learning her art by laughter.
masterman-ready-or-the-wreck-of-the-paci:
Frederick Marryat published Masterman Ready in 1841, for young people. Its full title adds Or, The Wreck of the Pacific. The tale opens in October, in a heavy gale at sea.

The Pacific runs before the wind in the wide Atlantic. Her captain watches the helm while waves lift and drop the ship. A lad of twelve clings to old Ready, the weather worn seaman. Ready calms the boy and tells him how a good ship rides a storm. Ready has sailed such seas for years and trusts the ship. His calm voice is the moral core Marryat built the tale round.
mount-music:
E. Œ. Somerville and Martin Ross published this Irish novel in 1920. The title page names both authors, though the catalog record credits Somerville alone. They were already known for The Real Charlotte and the Irish R.M. stories. The novel opens in a schoolroom, where young Christian Talbot-Lowry defies her bullying brother John.

Christian, nine in years and ninety in spirit, escapes to her father's hound kennels. She will not say she saw what she did not see, whatever the arm-twisting. The Lowry family's world of horses, hounds, and country houses fills the tale. Somerville and Ross write Irish gentry life with comedy and an undertow of loss.
nasa-tm-19630002685-heat-transfer-to-blu:
John O. Reller, Jr. of Ames Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-391, in 1960. It studies how heat flows into blunt, round-nosed bodies. Such bodies face the fierce heating of high-speed flight and reentry. A blunt nose spreads heat better than a sharp spike does.

Catalog notes say the work compares heat rates for bodies of revolution. It also weighs how the nose shape changes those heat rates. Designers of capsules and missiles needed such rates to size heat shields. Too much heat in one spot could burn through a hull. Reller's figures fed the blunt-body rule that shaped early American spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19630004028-a-wind-tunnel-invest:
Willard G. Smith of Ames Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-398, in February 1961. It reports wind tunnel tests of a reentry vehicle with folding wings. The wings could retract, or fold back, for the plunge through the air. Tests covered speeds below sound and just above it.

A blunt body survives reentry heat best, but it cannot fly well. Fold-out wings promised a craft that could glide and land after entry. Smith's tunnel runs checked stability and forces with wings out. The data weighed a bold trade: more parts and risk, for a runway landing. Such studies fed the long road toward reusable winged spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19640019815-characteristic-featu:
Wilton E. Causey of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this memorandum, TM X-53108, in August 1964. It studies repeating orbits in the Earth-Moon system. The setting is the restricted three body problem of classic mechanics. In that model, Earth and Moon pull on a much lighter craft.

Causey presents orbits that return to their start state in a rotating frame. He gives each orbit's period and its closest passes by Earth and Moon. Time spent between the two worlds is also listed. The orbits take one to four months per circuit. Each crosses the Earth-Moon line behind the Moon at least once. Such paths later mattered for Moon bases and relays.
nasa-tm-19660009105-magnetic-storms-in-t:
K W Behannon and Norman F Ness at Goddard wrote this October 1965 study of magnetic storms in Earth's magnetic tail. The tail is the long part of Earth's field stretched away from the Sun. It forms where the solar wind meets the geomagnetic field. The authors base their work on detailed measurements of the field at a range of distances, the abstract begins.

Storms in the tail store and release energy that reaches Earth. They disturb communications and can drive strong auroras. Satellite measurements in the tail itself were still new in 1965. Behannon and Ness use them to describe the storm process where it starts, rather than only its effects felt on the ground below.
nasa-tm-19660017356-electron-hydrogen-io:
A Temkin, in Goddard's Laboratory for Theoretical Studies, examined a subtle point in atomic theory in this February 4, 1966, paper. When an electron strikes a hydrogen atom hard enough, it can knock the atom's own electron free. That event is ionization. Temkin checks a wave function form proposed by Peterkop and by Rudge and Seaton for that process.

He finds that their form fails a required boundary condition. Far from the center, the error grows without limit, he shows. Temkin then turns to a zeroth order form from another theory. Threshold behavior, how the chance of ionization starts at the lowest energy, is the paper's second subject for specialists.
nasa-tm-19660021073-a-chain-matrix-analy:
A Goddard analysis dated July 19, 1965, works through a radar antenna problem with chain matrices. The antenna is a monopulse type, which senses aiming error in two planes at once by comparing signal strength. The technique under study scans the antenna's aim point, its boresight, by electronics rather than by motion. Chain matrices are a bookkeeping method that passes a signal through each part of a circuit in turn.

Electronic scanning gives fast, wear-free aiming for tracking antennas. The cost is complex circuitry whose errors must be predicted. A matrix analysis does that prediction in an orderly way. Tracking stations for the space program were the natural users of a dual-plane sensing design studied this carefully.
nasa-tm-19660026808-design-methods-for-m:
F. Edward McLean and Barrett L. Shrout, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, presented this paper at an Acoustical Society of America meeting in St. Louis in November 1965. Their topic is the sonic boom, the sharp pressure wave a fast airplane drags across the ground below.

The paper reviews theory-based design methods for weakening that boom. The methods shape the airplane itself to cut the pressure field's energy and peak pressure. The authors highlight a chance to reduce overpressure for large, slender airplanes, using their extended near-field behavior. They back the discussion with comparisons between theory and wind-tunnel measurements.
nasa-tm-19670030895-wind-tunnel-investig:
Bernard J. Blaha, Robert A. Wasko, and Donald L. Bresnahan, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, put a small Saturn model in a wind tunnel. The model copied the S-IC boost stage of the Saturn V. Two F-1 engine nozzles were fitted, and cold high-pressure air stood in for the exhaust jet.

The team measured the hinge moments that fight the engines' steering actuators. Base flow deflectors raised those moments, the tests showed. Moments peaked at the lower Mach numbers and eased as speed grew. Running the jet raised the moments compared with jet-off runs. Base pressures were recorded alongside, for the same deflector cases.
nasa-tm-19690007457-mean-gradient-heat-t:
James C. Hill wrote this January 1969 progress report, numbered X-641-69-6, on heat transfer in isotropic turbulence. Isotropic turbulence churns evenly in all directions, with no favored flow. Hill studies a steady fluid with a uniform average temperature gradient across it. The question is how the churning carries heat from warm side to cool.

Three ways of closing the statistical equations are discussed, ending with the direct-interaction approximation. That route needs a hard equation solved for an averaged response function. Hill tried the calculation in ordinary space coordinates first, as practice for harder shear flows. He reports plainly that numerical troubles defeated that attempt. The report closes with suggestions for finishing the work in wave-based coordinates.
nasa-tm-19690010296-an-exploratory-exper:
Separating two parallel lifting stages of a reusable launch vehicle is this thesis's subject. It is a master's thesis in aerospace engineering at the University of Virginia. The two stages fly side by side, then must part cleanly at three and six times the speed of sound. A collision or a tumbling stage at such speeds would end the mission.

Wind tunnel tests with models form the experimental half of the study. A computer program, written by Joseph Gera, tracks the vehicles' motion through the staging maneuver for the analytical half. Chapters describe the tunnel, models, and support gear, then the method of analysis. Experimental and numerical results are compared before the concluding remarks.
nasa-tm-19690011491-preliminary-developm:
Ramon M. Barnes of Lewis Research Center builds a new lab method for checking the makeup of superalloys in this report. The method uses a spark through a liquid layer on a solid sample. Barnes compares it with the standard point-to-plane spark method in air. Two test cobalt-base superalloys served for the checks.

Curves for the alloy parts shifted between the two methods. The liquid-layer method seemed to cut matrix effects for some elements. Close looks at samples and spectra hinted that mixed effects act as one to give that seeming cut. A side method with arc transfer gave true, steady results. The work aids tests of alloys used in hot engine parts.
nasa-tm-19690014794-apollo-saturn-5-flig:
Kennedy Space Center issued the Apollo/Saturn V Flight Safety Plan for vehicle AS-504 on February 22, 1969. Flight safety chief Arthur H. Moore and other program officials approved it. The plan states safety requirements, restrictions, and instrumentation for each launch. It covers the giant rocket from countdown through powered flight to orbit insertion.

Responsibility splits between the Air Force Eastern Test Range and Kennedy Space Center. The range commander sets flight termination requirements and protects life and property beyond the center. The center's director protects people and property inside Kennedy, clears launch danger areas, and owns crew safety. Requirements for destroying an errant vehicle and dispersing its propellant are also described.
nasa-tm-19690018463-cavitation-performan:
Phillip R. Meng and Royce D. Moore of Lewis Research Center evaluated a helical inducer in liquid hydrogen for this report. The 80.6-degree inducer ran at thirty thousand revolutions per minute. Tests covered a range of liquid hydrogen temperatures and flow coefficients, in both cavitating and noncavitating operation.

Net positive suction head needs fell as liquid temperature rose. At fixed temperature, those needs rose rapidly with flow coefficient. At low flow coefficients and higher temperatures, the inducer still produced useful head rise. It did so even with vapor present at its inlet. Such behavior matters for rocket turbopumps, which must keep feeding engines without losing prime in hydrogen service.
nasa-tm-19700019348-control-of-cell-divi:
Clarence D. Cone Jr. gave this presentation at the Twelfth Annual Science Writers Seminar in San Antonio, Texas, in March 1970. The seminar was run by the American Cancer Society. His topic is how the voltage across a cell's surface membrane controls whether that cell divides.

Cone argues that the ion pattern set by that voltage acts as a precise switch on division in body cells. He says the theory was tested and held up in work with mammalian cells. It also links cancer's two main dangers, uncontrolled growth and spreading, to one fault in the cell surface. Cells with strongly negative voltages, like nerve and muscle cells, seldom divide at all.
nasa-tm-19700023780-a-screening-and-sele:
Gerald Halpert of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in April 1970. It gives a screening and selection method for nickel-cadmium cell plates. Such plates sit at the heart of the rechargeable batteries that powered many spacecraft, so matched plates mattered for safe, even power.

Halpert's procedure sorts cell materials before assembly to improve uniformity and reliability across a batch. Screening by weight, he reports, proved a successful way to even out plate capacity. A statistical study of the test results shows a strong link between a plate's weight and its capacity. That link lets builders predict the capacity of every plate in a batch from weight alone.
nasa-tm-19710022873-new-directions-in-ma:
S S Manson of the Lewis Research Center gave this opening lecture at an August 1971 conference in Kyoto, Japan, on the mechanical behavior of materials. It surveys the harsh demands that coming machines would place on materials. His examples were car thermal reactors, jet engines, the space shuttle, and space nuclear power systems. Each project needed metals and plastics beyond the proven state of the art.

Manson showed recent research answering those demands. Topics ranged from new composite materials to powder metallurgy and directional solidification. He covered cold fracture and hot creep and fatigue as well. New test facilities and analysis methods featured throughout. The lecture mapped where materials research had to go next.
nasa-tm-19720016331-the-asee-university-:
This final report, numbered X-752-71-277, covers a summer faculty fellowship program at Goddard Space Flight Center. Its partners were the ASEE, the University of Maryland, and Catholic University. University faculty came to Goddard for about ten weeks at a time. The report marks the completion of the program's sixth year at Goddard.

At Goddard the fellows joined active research projects in their own fields and took part in seminars tied to that research. The stated aims include drawing universities into Goddard's research problems and keeping fellows researching after the summer ends. The program also aimed to stimulate Goddard staff through the exchanges and to build closer university ties. Contents cover administration, participants, the educational program, and the fellows' research reports, which open with studies of the SAS-A satellite.
nasa-tm-19720022697-average-daily-variat:
T L Skillman of NASA analyzed magnetic field readings from the ATS-5 satellite in this August 1972 report, NASA TM X-66004. ATS-5 sat in geostationary orbit, circling with Earth's rotation. Its magnetic field monitor recorded the field hour by hour. Skillman averaged those records to reveal the daily rhythm of the field. The data span two full years, from September 1969 through September 1971. Few studies then held such a complete record.

Hourly averages of each field component were sorted and studied. The sorting used levels of magnetic disturbance, ranked by the Kp index. Quiet days and stormy days show different daily patterns. Separating them shows how the field breathes with the solar wind. The report runs to fifty five pages. Its tables served magnetosphere modelers for years.
philip-winwood-a-sketch-of-the-domestic-: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of Philip Winwood, the publisher's list of Robert Neilson Stephens's works and the start of the full title. No chapter text is visible. The complete title describes a sketch of the domestic history of an American captain in the War of Independence. It covers events between and during 1763 and 1786 in New York and London. It claims to be written by his enemy in war, Herbert Russell, a lieutenant in the Loyalist forces.
podcast-joerogan-TukvVnadRic:
Schoolchildren in Zimbabwe who reported a UFO landing in 1994 are the subject of a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. At the Ariel School, dozens of young students told the same strange story of a craft and small beings. A Harvard professor later interviewed them on camera.

Rogan retells the case and weighs what makes it hard to shake: the number of witnesses, their agreement, and their calm years later as adults. He asks what else could explain that morning. The segment keeps one of the most debated UFO cases in circulation, told as a story first and a puzzle second.
public-lands-and-agrarian-laws-of-the-ro:
Andrew Stephenson, a professor of history at Wesleyan University, traced Rome's public lands from the earliest times to the founding of the Empire in a study printed at Baltimore in 1891. The work appeared in the Johns Hopkins University Studies in history and political science.

Stephenson follows the growth of private property in land, the swelling of the public domain by conquest, and its slow loss through sale, gifts, and colonies. Since grants of land required laws, the agrarian laws run through the whole story. Readers get a compact history of land, power, and reform in republican Rome.
shakespeare-and-music:
Edward W. Naylor published this study with J. M. Dent in London in 1896. Pictures drawn from the music of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries light up the text. Naylor holds degrees in arts and music, and he writes for readers who know the plays well but the old tunes less.

Songs, dances, and stage music run through Shakespeare's work, from catches and ballads to solemn measures. Naylor traces what those sounds were in Shakespeare's own day and how they worked in performance. The book helps modern readers hear the plays as their first crowds heard them, with period instruments and tunes restored to view.
sketches-of-western-north-carolina-histo:
C. L. Hunter wrote Sketches of Western North Carolina, Historical and Biographical, dated 1877. The book treats the war for freedom in Mecklenburg, Rowan, Lincoln, and nearby counties, with lives of the men who took part. Hunter states that much of the matter had never been printed before, and he adds mixed facts beyond the main war years.

Hunter opens by calling history a teacher that works through true examples. He argues that free states gain much when young men study the past. The war for freedom, in his view, shows weak colonies with no army, navy, or firm rule still standing up to the trained troops of a strong nation.
sonnets-on-sundry-notes-of-music:
Sonnets to Sundry Notes of Music carries William Shakespeare's name. The poems run in numbered sets. The first tells of a lording's daughter. She was the fairest of three sisters. Her fancy turned from her master to an Englishman. Long was the fight doubtful, love with love. One man of the two had to be refused. Art, with arms contending, won the day. The learned man bore the maid away.

The second poem hails a day in May. Love spied a blossom passing fair at play. The wind found passage through its velvet leaves. The lover wished himself the heaven's breath. He longed to blow on those cheeks as air does. His hand, though, has sworn off the flower. It will never pluck it from its thorn. A third piece turns to flocks that feed not.
tales-of-the-enchanted-islands-of-the-at:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote Tales of the Enchanted Islands of the Atlantic to retell old sea legends for new readers. In his preface he notes that Hawthorne had retold Greek myths in his Wonder Book, but no one had done the same for Atlantic island tales.

Higginson argues that early American lore is far from plain or dull, since each trip to the New World crossed a wild sea. He sees islands as places of magic, with height above depth and safe land beside storm. Readers get tales shaped over more than a thousand years, shared by both sides of the Atlantic as a joint birthright.
the-boy-aviators-polar-dash-or-facing-de: Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote The Boy Aviators' Polar Dash, or Facing Death in the Antarctic. A note in the book says Lawton is a pen name for John Henry Goldfrap. It is sixth in his Boy Aviators set. The first chapters are The Polar Ship, A Mysterious Robbery, and Off for the South Pole. Adrift on a Floating Island, Caught in the Flames, A Queer Accident, and The Professor is Kidnapped close the list shown.
the-republic: Plato's Republic imagines the just city ruled by philosopher-kings. The cave shadows. The Tower library holds the full text. It dreamed justice. Souls ordered. Kings philosophized. Truth reigned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-sisters-tragedy-with-other-poems-lyr: A volume of verse by Thomas Bailey Aldrich, the 19th-century American poet and editor of The Atlantic Monthly. The title poem is a dramatic tragedy in verse, and the rest range from tender lyrics to playful pieces, all polished in Aldrich's graceful, old-school style. It is a good window into the genteel American poetry that ruled magazines before the modernists arrived.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Developing a Computer Ethic forms part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Law alone cannot police the new machines. Older crafts like medicine had centuries to build their codes of conduct. Computing had only decades.

The piece argues for a clear code of right use. Computers now hold wealth that can move at a keystroke. They also carry out acts on their users' behalf. That dual role raises fresh blame questions. Both the firms that run systems and the people who use them need a sense of duty. Teaching should start in primary school and run through college. World guides from 1992 put respect for others' rights at the core.
